clue.text: Desperately wanting a 25% reduction in schoolwork

indicators.note: a reduction in the word means letters are cut from it

parts.note: giving lessons is the work done at a school
a quarter of an eight-letter word is two letters, here its first two

explanation.surface: A pupil longs to have a quarter less homework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'schoolwork' suggests homework, but it is the teacher's job. 'reduction in' cuts a quarter of its eight letters, TE, from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to yearn for it badly, so longing desperately fits.

clue.text: American not in play at the Globe (Merchant of Venice)

indicators.note: the words not in play about into a new order

parts.note: a globe is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: An American is absent from a performance at Shakespeare's Globe theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' rearranges NOT IN. 'Globe' looks like the London theatre but gives O. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the title character of Shakespeare's comedy, the Venetian trader who borrows from Shylock.

clue.text: See 13
Falls over a painter — get up!

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is a painter
to gain is to get

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles over an artist and is told to stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses A RA GAIN in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The great waterfalls on the US-Canada border are known simply by this name and the word falls.

clue.text: Moon an afterthought, Tramp admitted

indicators.note: the afterthought lets the tramp in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a postscript, PS, is an afterthought added to a letter
a hobo is a tramp or vagrant

explanation.surface: A vagrant gets let in at the last moment, almost as an afterthought.
explanation.walkthrough: An afterthought added to a letter is a postscript; 'admitted' signals the tramp going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the two small natural satellites orbiting Mars, an example of a moon.

clue.text: Spend time together in Chinese — stomach's empty

parts.note: the Han are China's majority ethnic group

indicators.note: the apostrophe s stands for has, so the stomach word has the other letter inside it

parts.note: gut is another word for the stomach
empty means holding nothing, the letter O

explanation.surface: Two people share a Chinese takeaway because their bellies are hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' reads as hungry but gives O, nothing; the 's (has) puts O inside GUT. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To loiter or socialise casually with friends is the colloquial sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Refuse to accommodate one woman over style not normally seen in public

definitions.text: style not normally seen in public

indicators.note: the refuse word takes the other letters into its middle

parts.note: bran is the husk discarded from grain, a kind of refuse

indicators.note: turned over, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one
Liza is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman is refused lodging over a hairstyle kept out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses the one-woman pieces and 'to accommodate' puts them inside the refuse word, after its second letter. The style is a full waxing of pubic hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A full bikini wax leaves an intimate style that is, by its nature, rarely displayed publicly.

clue.text: Particular place is affected

indicators.note: the letters are altered or disturbed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A certain location has been disturbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' rearranges PLACE IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Particular in the sense of specific or distinctive is a close synonym.

clue.text: That chap's very quiet round caged beasts

indicators.note: the possessive word is the cage holding the other letters

parts.note: his is the possessive for that chap
pp, pianissimo, means very quiet in music
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A man is hushed near some animals in cages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caged' signals the possessive word holding the rest; pp is the musical marking pianissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: These large African river animals are an example of beasts.

clue.text: Rewards of little value to the consumer

definitions.text: Rewards of little value to the consumer

parts.words: Rewards of little value to the consumer
parts.note: pay so low that the person who earns it, a consumer of food, can barely eat

explanation.surface: Points or perks that a shopper finds worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumer' reads as a shopper, but here it is someone who eats: pay too low to feed them.
explanation.definitionFit: Pay too meagre to live on is a fixed idiom for pitifully low earnings.

clue.text: Orange ladies include her

indicators.note: the words orange ladies contain her name across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A woman is among the members of a group of orange-clad ladies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'include' signals the name sitting inside 'Orange ladies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for a woman, and this is a common female first name.

clue.text: Constantly reproducing, much like anti-abortionists, I see

indicators.note: much of the word means most of it, here losing its final letter

parts.note: opponents of abortion describe their stance as pro-life
the word see sounds like the letter C

explanation.surface: Someone observes that anti-abortion campaigners are forever having children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much' drops the last letter of PROLIFE. 'see' gives C because the word is said like that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that keeps breeding or producing offspring in great numbers is fertile in exactly that sense.

clue.text: What those in authority earn?

parts.note: brass is slang for money, so the highest money is what senior people make; the phrase also names those senior people

explanation.surface: A question about the salaries of people in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is British slang for money, so the top money goes to the top people.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for the senior officers or managers who hold the most authority.

clue.text: Animals bred, in short, to run in sporting event

indicators.note: the letters run about and settle into new places, as loose animals would

explanation.surface: Livestock, bred to be compact, compete in an athletic contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run' rearranges ANIMALS BRED IN SHORT TO. The result is a three-day eventing competition held each year at an English country estate in Gloucestershire.
explanation.definitionFit: This annual equestrian competition is one of the best-known fixtures in British eventing.

clue.text: See 13
Pop's rejected about 500 — these people are pathetic

indicators.note: the reversed letters wrap round the numeral
turned back, so the word for pop is read from the end

parts.note: pop is fizzy soda, and with the 's it gives sodas
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: Dad's music is dismissed by his kids as tragic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns SODAS into SADOS; 'about' puts D (Roman 500) inside. 'Pop' looks like father but means soda.
explanation.definitionFit: Losers or sad cases is the British slang sense of the plural noun, people who are pitiful.

clue.text: Cheers about Queen's error — that's wrong

indicators.note: turned about, so the thanks word is read backwards

parts.note: ta is British for thanks, like cheers
Queen's Club in London hosts a tennis tournament, where an error on serve is a fault

explanation.surface: A toast celebrates around a monarch's blunder, which is bad form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses TA. Queen's Club is a London tennis venue with a major grass-court event.
explanation.definitionFit: Being to blame or in error is being in the wrong.

clue.text: Weird when retiring perfectly fit fighters

indicators.note: drawing back, so the pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd
as can mean when
A1 means first-rate, with the 1 written as I

explanation.surface: Strange how perfectly fit fighters withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' reverses RUM AS to SAMUR; A1, first-class, is written AI.
explanation.definitionFit: These were the warrior class of feudal Japan, an example of fighters.

clue.text: No wild enthusiasm amongst sailors for Vlad?

indicators.note: the pieces sit among the sailors, inside their two letters

parts.note: RN, the Royal Navy, stands for sailors
nothing, a zero, the letter O
a mania is a wild craze

explanation.surface: No frenzy among the crew for the sinister prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amongst' signals the insertion. Vlad the Impaler ruled Wallachia, now in Romania; Vlad is also this puzzle's setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vlad the Impaler is the famous historical ruler from that Balkan nation, a definition by example.

clue.text: Sporting legend about to get beat

parts.note: re means about or concerning
to drum is to beat

explanation.surface: A sports hero is about to be defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the racehorse that won the Grand National, Britain's great steeplechase, three times in the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: That steeplechaser is a legend of British horse racing, so a sporting legend by example.

clue.text: Artist's model turned up in same shot

indicators.note: the reversed letters go inside the rearranged ones
shot means broken or ruined, so the letters are rearranged
in a down entry this reads the letters upwards, reversed

parts.note: to sit is to model for an artist

explanation.surface: A painter's model appeared in the same photo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reverses the model word; 'shot' scrambles the same word; 'in' puts the first inside the second. 'model' looks like a noun but is the verb to pose.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a leading French painter of the Fauvist movement, an example of an artist.

clue.text: Don't they like to see people getting on?

definitions.text: Don't they like to see people getting on?

parts.words: Don't they like to see people getting on?
parts.note: getting on usually means getting along, but here means growing old; these people dislike the elderly

explanation.surface: A question about those who resent people being friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting on' seems to mean getting along together; it means growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people prejudiced against others because of their age.

clue.text: Maintained an agent to guard stable

indicators.note: the agent surrounds and protects the stable word

parts.note: a fed is an American federal agent
firm means steady or stable

explanation.surface: An officer is assigned to protect a racing stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stable' reads as a horses' yard but means steady; 'to guard' signals the agent surrounding it.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain a claim is to assert it, the same as declaring it confidently.

clue.text: Doctor has row about building material

indicators.note: the row goes round the doctor's letters

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A physician argues over what to build with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' reads as a quarrel but means a line of seats; 'about' signals it going round the doctor's degree letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Wood cut and prepared for construction is a classic material for building.

clue.text: Keen runner has easy run

parts.note: Mo Farah, the British Olympic distance champion, is the runner

indicators.note: taken easy or loosely, the letters are relaxed into a new order

explanation.surface: An eager athlete enjoys a gentle jog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like eager but is the old verb to lament; 'runner' is Mo Farah, Britain's Olympic 5,000m and 10,000m champion. 'easy' rearranges RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to wail in grief over the dead, the same as lamenting a loss.

clue.text: Fruit spread off your trolley? Question remains

parts.note: butter is spread on bread
British slang for crazy, as is nuts
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A shopper asks what is left of the fruit spread in their trolley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off your trolley' is British slang for mad; a trolley is a supermarket cart.
explanation.definitionFit: This pear-shaped winter gourd is botanically a fruit, though cooked as a vegetable.

clue.text: Kissing isn't silent? No worries

indicators.note: the letters are troubled and pulled about into a new order

explanation.surface: Kissing is never quiet? Don't fret about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worries' rearranges ISNT SILENT NO; 'No worries' looks like a set phrase, but 'No' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: This is jokey slang for deep, open-mouthed kissing, likened to a game played with the throat.
